summary: Describes how Ethernet VLANs, commonly used to separate traffic in enterprise networks, can be used to deploy IPv6 early, before switch-routers support it. It addresses coexistence of IPv4 and IPv6 in the same enterprise. This is informational guidance.

plainLanguage.summary: A company wants to try a new kind of address without breaking the old one. This shows how to keep them in separate lanes of the same network so both work.

questions: how to deploy ipv6 with vlans
subtitle: Using virtual LANs to deploy IPv6 in enterprises before dual-stack routers are available.

tldr.problem: Enterprises want to deploy IPv6 early, but their core network equipment does not yet support IPv6. They cannot simply upgrade all their routers immediately.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes using Ethernet VLANs to deploy a parallel IPv6 routing infrastructure. A single IPv6 router can serve multiple subnets via VLAN tags, while existing IPv4 routers continue to handle IPv4. Both operate on the same physical network infrastructure.
tldr.outcome: Enterprises can deploy IPv6 in a structured, managed way to some or all of their network in advance of their core infrastructure supporting it, using a method already proven at multiple research sites.

today: RFC 4554 is an Informational memo describing a method for IPv6 deployment that was already in use at multiple research sites. Today, most enterprises have native IPv6 support in their equipment, but this technique remains a valid approach for staged IPv6 adoption and is still documented as a reference for dual-stack deployment.

sections.title: Early IPv6 Deployment Using VLANs
sections.content:
Ethernet VLANs (Virtual LANs) allow separate logical LANs to be deployed over a single bridged physical LAN by inserting VLAN tagging or membership information into Ethernet frames. This document describes how sites already using VLANs can exploit this technology to deploy IPv6 early, before their core switch-router equipment supports IPv6 natively.

The method uses a parallel IPv6 routing infrastructure (likely a separate platform from the site's existing equipment) that handles IPv6 traffic. The IPv6 router connects to a VLAN-capable switch and routes IPv6 traffic in parallel with existing IPv4. No changes to IPv4 configuration are required. The IPv4 default route is provided by one router while the IPv6 default route is provided by a different IPv6 router.

The IPv6 connectivity entering the site may be native or tunneled from the provider. This technique has been adopted by multiple sites including research networks.
sections.plainLanguage: If your building's mail system (the IPv4 network) is working fine, you can add a new mail system (IPv6) that uses the same hallways. They keep their mail separate with colored labels (VLANs) so they do not mix up.

sections.title: How IPv6 Routing Works Over VLANs
sections.content:
In a typical deployment, one IPv6 router has an external interface to the wider IPv6 Internet and one or more internal interfaces. The external interface may be dual-stack (using tunneling) or IPv6-only (using native connectivity).

The internal interface connects directly to a VLAN-capable switch. The router writes VLAN tags on packets sent from the internal interface based on the target IPv6 link prefix. The VLAN-tagged traffic is then transported across the internal VLAN-capable infrastructure to the target IPv6 links, which may be dispersed widely across the site.

When the IPv6 router cannot VLAN-tag packets itself, a protocol-based VLAN can be created on the VLAN-capable device connected to the router, causing IPv6 traffic to be tagged and redistributed on (congruent) IPv4 subnet links that lie in the same VLAN.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPv6 router puts a special label on each message saying which department it is for. The network switches read these labels and deliver the message to the right place, even though everything goes through the same wires.

sections.title: Deployment Topologies
sections.content:
There are several ways to deploy IPv6 over VLANs depending on site needs and equipment.

One VLAN per router interface: A site with three internal IPv6 links could use a standard PC-based IPv6 router with one external port and three internal ports (one per link). One switch port is needed per link. IPv6 routing can be cascaded through lower-tier internal IPv6-only routers, with edge router ports feeding other IPv6 routers over IPv6-only links.

Collapsed VLANs on a single interface: Many devices now support VLAN tagging based on virtual interfaces, allowing multiple IPv6 VLANs to be assigned (trunked) from a single physical router interface. This is more practical for sites planning to introduce IPv6 to part of their network. As traffic volume grows, the single interface can be extended to use two or more physical ports.

Congruent IPv4 and IPv6 subnets: Most enterprises want dual-stack IPv4-IPv6 networking. The IPv6 connectivity can be injected into existing IPv4 VLANs such that IPv4 and IPv6 subnets are exactly congruent. This has desirable administrative properties: devices in each IPv4 subnet are in the same IPv6 subnet. IPv6-only devices can be gradually added without needing to resize the IPv6 subnet (which can hold effectively infinite hosts in a /64, compared to limited IPv4 subnet sizes).
sections.plainLanguage: There are different ways to set this up. You can give one special port on the router to each department. Or you can put multiple departments on one port with fancy labeling. Or you can mix IPv4 and IPv6 traffic on the same label and let routers separate them.

sections.title: Addressing and Configuration
sections.content:
IPv6 addressing in VLAN-based deployments follows standard IPv6 practices. One site using this technique has chosen to number its IPv6 links with the format [Site IPv6 prefix]:[VLAN ID]::/64, where the VLAN tag (16 bits) becomes part of the address. While this linking of VLAN ID into an addressing scheme may not fit topology and aggregation best practices, some sites may find it useful.

As sites transition to dual-stack, when IPv6-capable switch-router equipment is acquired, the VLAN-based method can continue to be used, just as it is commonly used today for IPv4 subnets, but then with a common IPv4-IPv6 routing infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Each department gets a range of IPv6 addresses for its subnet. Some sites put the department number (VLAN ID) into the address itself, though this is not required.

sections.title: Security and Final Deployment
sections.content:
There are no additional security considerations particular to the VLAN-based method of enabling IPv6 on a link beyond normal considerations.

However, where IPv6 connectivity enters the enterprise via a different path from IPv4, care must be taken to apply equivalent security policy to the IPv6 path. Firewalling and intrusion detection should be configured for the IPv6 access link just as they are for IPv4. The IPv6 router will require additional infrastructure and costs, and often requires a separate link from an IPv6 provider.

This VLAN technique offers a more structured alternative to opportunistic per-host tunneling methods such as ISATAP (Intra-Site Automatic Tunnel Addressing Protocol), providing a simple yet efficient method for early IPv6 deployment in an enterprise.
sections.plainLanguage: Remember to protect the IPv6 path with the same security rules as IPv4. The new router needs its own connection to the outside, which costs money. But once you have it, you have a cleaner way to run both types of networks together.
